questions.stem: Which of the following defines ELINT?
questions.key: A SIGINT sub-discipline dedicated to collecting and analysing non-communication signals
distractors: A SIGINT sub-discipline dedicated to collecting and analysing voice and data messages
An EW function dedicated to searching, intercepting and locating emitters for the commander
An EW function dedicated to attacking enemy radars so that friendly forces can operate
questions.explanation: The deck quotes PAM 3-0702-01: ELINT is a SIGINT sub-discipline for the collection and technical analysis of non-communication electromagnetic signals.
why: Voice and data messages belong to COMINT, not ELINT.
Searching, intercepting and locating for the commander is the ES role within EW, not an ELINT definition.
Attacking radars is Electronic Attack (EA), not ELINT.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the Adversary Electronic Order of Battle?
questions.key: The location, frequency and characteristics of hostile radios and weapon-guidance radars, used to drive targeting and plan countermeasures
distractors: A catalogue of the unit's own radios, radars, data links and navigation aids, used to prevent mutual interference and protect OPSEC
A catalogue of civilian and commercial emitters, used to avoid hitting civilians and to stay within telecom agreements
A growing record set of every intercept, kept as a mugshot book of enemy radars
questions.explanation: The Adversary EOB holds hostile radios and weapon-guidance radars and is used to drive targeting and plan countermeasures; ELINT's main job is to fill and update it.
why: That is the Friendly EOB.
That is the Neutral EOB.
That is the signature library, which feeds the EOB rather than being an EOB.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes ES when the lesson compares it with ELINT?
questions.key: The backup camera: real time, perishable and owned by the tactical commander
distractors: The black-box recorder: deliberate, long-term and owned by intelligence channels
The targeting board: where the commander matches emitters with responses
The signature library: a growing record of every intercept
questions.explanation: The deck calls ES the commander's backup camera and ELINT the intelligence black-box recorder; the same receiver serves a different purpose.
why: That describes ELINT, not ES.
The targeting board is the decision forum that uses ES data, not ES itself.
The signature library is where ELINT and ES records are kept, not a description of ES.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the one-way advantage?
questions.key: The receiver needs only the outbound trip of the pulse, so a radar can usually be detected from beyond its own range
distractors: The radar needs only the weak echo back, so it can detect our post from beyond our receiver's range
The time between the outgoing pulse and its returning echo gives the range to the target
A passive receiver emits nothing, so its site can never be given away
questions.explanation: A radar needs its weak echo over a two-way trip, while the ES receiver needs only the outbound trip, so it can usually detect the radar from farther than the radar can see.
why: That reverses the advantage; it is the receiver, not the radar, that benefits from the one-way trip.
That is the radar sequence of pulse out, echo back, time equals range.
The deck warns that our own radios, vehicles and lights can still give a site away.

questions.stem: It is the fingerprint parameter that gives the number of pulses a radar sends each second, equal to 1 divided by the PRI.
distractors: Pulse width (PW)
Pulse repetition interval (PRI)
Carrier frequency (Ft)
questions.explanation: PRF is pulses per second and equals 1 divided by PRI, so a PRI of 1 ms is a PRF of 1 kHz.
why: PW is how long each individual pulse lasts.
PRI is the time between pulses, the reciprocal of PRF.
Ft is the carrier frequency, which tells you the band.

questions.stem: It is the growing reference of enemy radars to which every intercept adds a record, like a mugshot book.
distractors: The targeting board
The waterfall display
The Neutral EOB
questions.explanation: Each new intercept is recorded in the signature library, which is validated and shared to feed the EOB.
why: The targeting board is where the commander decides how to respond to identified emitters.
The waterfall display shows signals over time; it is not a record set.
The Neutral EOB catalogues civilian and commercial emitters.

questions.stem: An ES team sees a waterfall trace that is a steady line staying on at one position. Which source does the lesson read this as?
questions.key: A beacon or radio left on
distractors: Someone talking
Data traffic
A rotating radar
questions.explanation: Slide 4 reads a steady line as a beacon or radio left on. Irregular bursts are someone talking, wideband bursts are data traffic, and evenly spaced short hits are a rotating radar.
why: Talking appears as irregular bursts, not a steady line.
Data traffic appears as many short wideband bursts, not a steady line.
A rotating radar appears as short, evenly spaced hits, not a steady line.

questions.stem: An ES operator sees a radar whose beam holds steady on a target, with a higher PRF and a shorter PW. Which reading does the lesson give?
questions.key: Track: the radar is following a target
distractors: Search: the radar is looking around the area
Circular scan: a 360° sweep of the whole area
Sector scan: sweeping back and forth over an area of interest
questions.explanation: Slide 16 reads a steady beam on the target with a higher PRF and a shorter PW as track.
why: Search is a rotating or sector scan with a lower PRF and a longer PW.
A circular scan sweeps all round; it is not a steady beam on one target.
A sector scan moves back and forth; it is not a steady beam on one target.

questions.stem: At 0312H an ES team notes that an emitter has switched from sweeping the area to a steady beam with a higher PRF. What does the lesson say the team should do?
questions.key: Report the switch from search to track immediately
distractors: Hold the report until a second fix is obtained
Wait for the signature library to confirm the identity first
File the change in the log and report it at the end of the shift
questions.explanation: A switch from search to track on the same emitter is reported immediately.
why: The lesson attaches no such delay to the switch report.
Identity can stay tentative while the behaviour change is reported.
A change in intent is time-sensitive and is not held for the end of the shift.

questions.stem: An ES squad logs a radar that detects incoming shells and computes where the gun fired from. Which ground emitter is this?
distractors: Ground-surveillance radar
Coastal radar
Short-range air-surveillance radar
questions.explanation: The weapon-locating radar detects incoming shells and computes the gun position, so it is a threat to our artillery.
why: Ground-surveillance radar detects people and vehicles moving at range.
Coastal radar raises the question of whether a contact is friendly, civil or foreign.
Short-range air-surveillance radar threatens helicopters and drones.

questions.stem: An ES squad logs a new emitter at 9.41 GHz. In which NATO band does this place it?
distractors: J-band (10 to 20 GHz)
K-band (above 20 GHz)
H-band (below 8 GHz)
questions.explanation: The carrier frequency tells you the band, and I-band runs from 8 to 10 GHz, which includes 9.41 GHz.
why: J-band starts at 10 GHz, above this emitter.
K-band starts at 20 GHz, well above this emitter.
H-band lies below 8 GHz, under this emitter.

questions.stem: Which list gives the five steps of the ES and ELINT process in order?
questions.key: Search and Detect; Locate and Track; Analyse; Evaluate; Collate and Report
distractors: Search and Detect; Locate and Track; Evaluate; Analyse; Collate and Report
Locate and Track; Search and Detect; Analyse; Evaluate; Collate and Report
Search and Detect; Analyse; Locate and Track; Evaluate; Collate and Report
questions.explanation: The deck orders the steps as Search and Detect, Locate and Track, Analyse, Evaluate, then Collate and Report.
why: Evaluate cannot come before Analyse: a signature must be measured before it is matched.
A radar must be found before it can be located and tracked.
Locate and Track comes before the fingerprint is analysed.

questions.stem: Which list contains the three Electronic Orders of Battle named in PAM 3-0702-01 as taught in this lesson?
distractors: Friendly, Adversary and Allied
Friendly, Hostile and Civil
Adversary, Neutral and Coalition
questions.explanation: Slides 9 and 24 name the Friendly, Adversary and Neutral EOBs; Neutral covers civilian and commercial emitters.
why: Allied is not one of the three EOBs; the third is Neutral.
Hostile and Civil are not the EOB names; they are Adversary and Neutral.
Coalition is not an EOB, and the Friendly EOB is omitted.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the radar fingerprint parameters in the lesson?
distractors: Polarization
Beamwidth
Pulse width
questions.explanation: The fingerprint covers carrier frequency, scan, PW, beamwidth, PRI/PRF, polarization, and modulation and bandwidth. Receiver sensitivity is a property of the listening equipment, not of the radar.
why: Polarization, the orientation of the wave, is a fingerprint parameter.
Beamwidth is a fingerprint parameter.
Pulse width is a fingerprint parameter.

questions.stem: Which statement about ELINT is NOT supported by the lesson?
questions.key: ELINT is owned by the tactical commander for real-time threat warning
distractors: ELINT sits within SIGINT beside COMINT
ELINT's main job is filling and updating the Adversary EOB
ELINT examines radars, beacons and sensors
questions.explanation: Ownership by the tactical commander for real-time, perishable warning describes ES. ELINT is the black-box recorder owned by intelligence channels.
why: The deck places ELINT in SIGINT, the intelligence arm, beside COMINT.
Filling and updating the Adversary EOB is ELINT's main job.
The deck pairs ELINT with radars, beacons and sensors.
